examples.problem_statement: There are four numbers w, x, y, z. If the sum of all possible distinct groups, each having two numbers from amongst w, x, y, z is 1440, then what is the average of these four numbers?

solution.description: List every distinct group of two numbers that can be formed from w, x, y, z; there are six such groups.

solution.result: each of w, x, y, z appears 3 times in the total
solution.description: Write the given total as the sum of those six groups written out term by term, and notice each letter occurs three times across the list.
Factor the repeated count of 3 out of the expanded sum and divide 1440 by 3 to get the plain sum of the four numbers.
Divide that sum of the four numbers by 4 to get their average.

key_reminders: Each of the four numbers appears in exactly 3 of the 6 distinct pairs, so the pairwise total equals 3 times the plain sum.
Average = (sum of the numbers) / (count of the numbers).
common_mistakes: Dividing 1440 by 4 straight away and reporting 360, forgetting that the pairwise total counts every number three times.
Counting ordered pairs (12 of them) instead of the 6 distinct two-number groups, which halves the multiplier.

examples.problem_statement:
Six doctors—Haddad, Johnson, Kwong, Lester, Murray, and Nelson—are assigned to the following three training rotations: orthopedics, pediatrics, surgery. Each doctor is assigned to exactly one rotation, and each rotation is assigned exactly two doctors. No other doctors are assigned. The following conditions must be met: Kwong is not assigned to the same rotation as Lester. Murray is not assigned to surgery. If Lester is assigned to orthopedics, then Haddad is assigned to surgery. Johnson is assigned to surgery.

It can be determined to which rotation each of the six doctors is assigned if which one of the following statements is true?
(A) Both Murray and Kwong are assigned to orthopedics.
(B) Both Kwong and Nelson are assigned to pediatrics.
(C) Both Haddad and Johnson are assigned to surgery.
(D) Both Johnson and Lester are assigned to surgery.
(E) Both Haddad and Nelson are assigned to pediatrics.

solution.result: the conditional rule is the rule most likely to break the question open
solution.description: Instead of testing answers by trial and error, single out the major conditional rule and hunt for the answer choices that engage it directly.

Check (C): it places H in surgery, which is the back end of the conditional and cannot be read backwards, and its other placement, J in surgery, is already known — so it wastes one of the two placements the answer gives you.

solution.operation: \text{test (E): } H \to P,\; N \to P \;\Rightarrow\; H \nrightarrow S \;\Rightarrow\; L \nrightarrow O
solution.description: Move to (E): putting H in pediatrics triggers the contrapositive of the conditional, because H not being in surgery forces L out of orthopedics.

solution.operation: P = \{H, N\},\; M \nrightarrow S \;\Rightarrow\; M \to O
solution.description: With pediatrics already filled by H and N, and M forbidden from surgery, the only rotation left for M is orthopedics.

solution.operation: L \nrightarrow O,\; L \nrightarrow P \;\Rightarrow\; L \to S
solution.result: L joins surgery and the diagram is complete
solution.description: Since L cannot be in orthopedics and pediatrics is full, L must go to surgery — at which point every doctor's rotation is fixed, which is exactly what the question asks for.

key_reminders: A conditional rule runs one way only — satisfying its result does not let you conclude its trigger.
The contrapositive of 'if L is in orthopedics then H is in surgery' is 'if H is not in surgery then L is not in orthopedics'.
Each of the three rotations takes exactly two doctors, so filling one rotation removes it as an option for everyone else.
common_mistakes: Reading the conditional backwards in (C) and concluding that H in surgery forces L into orthopedics.
Picking an answer that spends one of its two placements on J in surgery, a placement the rules already fixed.
